narrative:
The model predicts you will fail your final year, with an estimated chance of about one in three. That is not a certainty, but under the rule used here it is enough to classify you as at risk of failing and to require remedial courses before final results.

The strongest factor pushing toward that prediction is that you do not want to pursue higher education; among students who passed, every one wanted to continue studying. The next two most influential factors actually worked in your favour. You have no past class failures, matching the average passer, and your 30–60 minute commute—longer than most passers, only about 5% of whom travel that long—was treated as slightly protective. So the concern is mainly low intention to continue education, not a history of failing.

Other profile points add risk: you study under two hours weekly while most passers study two to five; you have 8 absences versus an average of 3.78; you lack home internet when 81% of passers have it; and you report very high going out and weekend alcohol use. To improve, use remedial courses to build a steady study routine, attend consistently, access school or library internet, and connect your current work to a concrete next step in education. Protect your no-failure record—it is a real strength.
